source.title: DiRe: Dispersing Refusal Vectors to Defend Against Open-Source LLM Abliteration
source.citation: DiRe: Dispersing Refusal Vectors to D…

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies difference-in-means direction extraction and projection or subtraction attacks, then reports refusal retention. It also tests multidirectional removal and representational geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports values used to tune its method and extensive additional evaluations. Rows below focus on direct direction-removal results, multidirectional attacks, and geometry relevant to the claim. The main single-direction retention results are five-dataset averages; some additional AdvBench results are kept separately because they use a different prompt set. Capability benchmarks are reported, but they evaluate DiRe training rather than general capability after direction ablation, so they do not directly test that part of V1. The study does not test adding the direction or jailbreaks that suppress it.
record.test_reason: On the released (Original) checkpoints, the paper re-runs the original method. It extracts a difference-in-means direction at the last post-instruction token, then projects it out of the weights or subtracts it from activations. It reports refusal retention on five harmful sets with two judges. It also measures deviation geometry and multi-directional attacks, and compares base with instruct checkpoints. Most results concern its own DiRe defense, which bears on V4 and V7 rather than on V1 in standard models. Adding the direction, and capability after ablation itself, are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also attribute the concentration that abliteration exploits to alignment training (base vs instruct comparison). They say DiRe raises the cost of abliteration but does not prevent it, and that it lowers general capability in all three families and raises over-refusal on Mistral.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means extraction and residual-stream direction removal, with retention measured after projection and subtraction. The study primarily evaluates a newly trained dispersion defense rather than reproducing the original causal ablation and addition tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model family, attack type, evaluation dataset, judge, extraction layer, and defense weights. GPT-5 retention on Phi under projection is particularly low on some datasets; multidirectional attacks and output coherence also change interpretation.
record.problems: The paper reports one main training run per defense for its repeated-judge analysis; its five-run comparison has limited precision. Defense weights are tuned separately by model. The threat model extracts at the last post-instruction token, leaving other positions untested. Some multidirectional retention is conditional on coherent outputs, and the authors caution about survivorship bias; the Phi cross-layer rank-16 condition has only 33 coherent outputs out of 500. The paper also says its captured-energy analysis is descriptive and does not establish a causal link to refusal retention.
record.rows_left_out: Not all per-dataset values from Table 5, all rank-4 and rank-8 subspace results in Tables 13–15, the full layer sweeps in Figure 4, or the complete auxiliary ablation and weight-sweep tables were extracted. The selected rows prioritize aggregate single-direction tests, multidirectional conditions, geometry measures, and base-versus-instruct comparison; other omitted values are further breakdowns of these settings.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; general capability after ablation of the Original models.
Not tested at all. DiRe trains for dispersion, not against jailbreaks.
Timing of refusal training; controlled comparison of standard training procedures.

missing.what: Clean versus attacked AdvBench refusal for Original under projection and subtraction (Llama .92→.03/.13; Mistral .70→.11/.06; Phi 1.00→.01/.07). This is the direct V1/V2 baseline.
Layer dependence of single-direction removal on Original. Retention is high outside the middle layers, e.g. Llama 0.66–0.82 at L14–16 on AdvBench.
Residual energy after removing the single direction in Original: rho = 17/34/18% for Llama/Mistral/Phi.
Original under the SOM multi-directional attack (.02/.01, .05/.02, .09/.00). Mean pairwise cosine of SOM directions in Original Llama is 0.25.
Refusal Jacobian Rank for Original (erank 5.43/5.54/3.57; srank 1.52/1.65/1.30): dimensionality of the refusal-logit gradient.
Harmful compliance and coherent counts for Original after the attacks (e.g. Llama projection H .75, 349/500 coherent).

record.verdict_notes: Most rows are the study's own defense or prior defenses. Only the Original checkpoints replicate the original finding, so V1/V2 verdicts rest on those. DiRe results are evidence that training shapes removability (V7) and that dispersed refusal needs multi-direction removal (V4), but via an objective built for that purpose. Coherent-only subspace retention (r31-r39) is subject to survivorship bias, as the authors warn. Base vs instruct evidence (r47-r48) is figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: Tests refusal after difference-in-means direction removal, but not adding the direction; does not measure general capability after the ablation itself.
No practical weight edit on released models is evaluated as abliteration.
Does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the direction or whether training specifically against its ablation adds robustness.
Tests dispersion and multidirectional removal in these models, but does not establish that naturally occurring refusal is generally better described by an affine rule or cone.
No separate harmfulness-judgment and refusal-decision measurement.
No transfer of an extracted direction across languages or model variants, and no attack transfer from base to instruct models.
Compares pretrained base and instruction-tuned geometry for two families; does not isolate training timing or compare controlled refusal-training procedures.
